title: Your day, in detail
job: Longer habitual narration with sequencing words
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: REFLEXIVE VERBS ARE A SYSTEM, and this is where the shape gets said out loud. A particle rides on the very end of the verb, after the ordinary personal ending: -s' when that ending finishes in a vowel (prosypáyu + s' = prosypáyus'), -sya when it finishes in a consonant (prosypáyet + sya = prosypáyetsya). That spelling choice is the whole of the rule, and the ending underneath never changes to accommodate it.

THE PARTICLE DOES NOT ALWAYS MEAN "MYSELF". umyváyus' really is "I wash myself" and odeváyus' "I dress myself", but vozvrashcháyus' ("I come back") has no self to act on and lozhús' ("I lie down") has none either. English reads the reflexive and hunts for the object; Russian is mostly just marking that the verb takes none. Learn the verb whole, and do not translate the -s' each time.

nikogdá REQUIRES A SECOND NEGATIVE. Russian says Ya nikogdá ne p'yu kófe — literally "I never not drink coffee" — and the ne is not optional, not emphatic and not a mistake. English forbids exactly this pairing, so an English speaker builds Ya nikogdá p'yu and hears nothing wrong; a Russian hears a sentence that stopped halfway. The two negatives agree here rather than cancelling.

The frequency words are ordinary adverbs and they sit in front of the verb, or open the sentence: obýchno, chásto, inogdá, rédko, vsegdá, nikogdá. Only nikogdá changes anything around it. Parking one at the end, the way English parks "usually", makes it an afterthought rather than a fact.

The sequencing spine of a day is snachála … potóm … zatém … nakonéts. Three quarters of it is already yours — snachála from L2-M10, potóm from L1-M10 — and only zatém and nakonéts are new. They are all free words: nothing about them differs from first, then, next, finally.

Every clause in this module is present and imperfective, because a day that repeats is not a story. The past is L1-M5's and L2-M10's business, and aspect at length is L3-M10's; here the tense simply never changes, which is what lets an item run to two sentences without getting harder.

sentences.cue: I wake up early every day

words.note: The -s' is the reflexive particle, glued on after the ordinary -yu ending. There is no bare prosypáyu to fall back on: the verb only exists with its particle.

sentences.trap: prosypáyus' is opening your eyes, not leaving the bed. L1-M4's vstayú is the getting-up verb, and a Russian account of a morning usually names both in that order.
sentences.sound: pra-sy-PA-yus RA-na KAZH-dyy dyen. The stress is on the -pá- and the particle takes none of it — every reflexive in this module behaves that way.

variations.cue: I wake up late every day
Usually I wake up early
variations.changed: a frequency word in place of every day

mistake.why: Dropping the particle leaves a different verb altogether — prosypát' is to spill something. Ya prosypáyus' ráno kázhdyy den'.

sentences.usage: Answering what your morning looks like.
sentences.mnemonic: The self rides on the end.

sentences.cue: First I wash, then I get dressed

words.note: One of the few where the particle really is "myself": umyváyu something else, umyváyus' myself. It means the face and hands, not a bath.
Same particle, same job: odeváyu a child, odeváyus' myself. Russian never says the clothes here — Ya odeváyus' is the complete sentence.

sentences.trap: The second clause drops ya and keeps the particle. What a Russian clause may leave out is the pronoun; what it may never leave out is the -s'.
sentences.sound: sna-CHA-la ya u-my-VA-yus, pa-TOM a-dye-VA-yus. Both verbs are stressed on their -vá- syllable, one step before the particle.

variations.cue: First I wash, then I have breakfast
variations.changed: breakfast in place of getting dressed

variations.cue: First I wash, next I get dressed

mistake.why: Without the particle both verbs are waiting for an object you never gave them. Snachála ya umyváyus', potóm odeváyus'.

sentences.usage: Listing the first two things you do in the morning.
sentences.mnemonic: Wash yourself, dress yourself — both end in -s'.

sentences.display: Obýchno ya závtrakayu v sem' chasóv
sentences.script: Обычно я завтракаю в семь часов
sentences.cue: Usually I have breakfast at seven o'clock
sentences.literal: Usually I breakfast at seven of-hours

words.note: The plain, high-frequency "usually". It opens a sentence as comfortably as it sits before the verb, and it carries no shade of surprise the way "normally" can.
Breakfast is a VERB in Russian, so there is no noun in the sentence to eat. The stress sits on the first syllable and never moves off it.

sentences.trap: There is no word for "breakfast" in this sentence and none is missing — závtrakayu is the whole predicate. Adding a noun for the meal is how an English speaker overbuilds it.
sentences.sound: a-BYCH-na ya ZAV-tra-ka-yu f syem cha-SOF. závtrakayu has four unstressed syllables trailing its stress, and every one of them reduces.

variations.cue: Sometimes I have breakfast at a café
variations.changed: sometimes, and out at a café

variations.cue: Usually I have breakfast at home

mistake.display: Obýchno ya iméyu závtrak v sem' chasóv
mistake.script: Обычно я имею завтрак в семь часов
mistake.why: Two English habits at once: a noun for the meal and a verb for having, neither of which Russian uses here. Obýchno ya závtrakayu v sem' chasóv.

sentences.usage: Describing the shape of a normal morning.

sentences.display: Zatém ya idú na rabótu peshkóm
sentences.script: Затем я иду на работу пешком
sentences.literal: Next I go to work on-foot

words.note: The step-after-the-step word. potóm is the everyday "then"; zatém is the same move inside a list you are counting through, and a shade more written.

sentences.trap: idú is already going on foot, and peshkóm only makes it explicit. Attached to a vehicle verb it would contradict it, which is why L2-M4 taught the two together.
sentences.sound: za-TYEM ya i-DU na ra-BO-tu pyesh-KOM. Four of the five words carry their stress on the last syllable, which gives the line its forward push.

variations.display: Potóm ya idú na rabótu peshkóm
variations.script: Потом я иду на работу пешком
variations.cue: Then I walk to work
variations.changed: potóm, the everyday word, in place of zatém

variations.cue: Next I come back home

mistake.display: Zatém ya idú na rabóta peshkóm
mistake.script: Затем я иду на работа пешком
mistake.why: na with a destination takes the accusative, as L2-M4 taught. Zatém ya idú na rabótu peshkóm.

sentences.usage: Walking someone through the middle of your morning.

sentences.display: Ya nikogdá ne p'yu kófe vécherom
sentences.script: Я никогда не пью кофе вечером
sentences.cue: I never drink coffee in the evening
sentences.literal: I never not drink coffee in-the-evening

words.note: It never stands alone: the verb still takes ne in front of it. Ya nikogdá ne p'yu — two negatives that agree rather than cancel.

sentences.trap: The literal line is the lesson. Russian says "I never not drink", and an English speaker who trusts English deletes the ne and produces a sentence that stops halfway.
sentences.sound: ni-kag-DA nye PYU KO-fye VYE-cha-ram. nikogdá is stressed on its last syllable, exactly like the kogdá buried inside it.

variations.cue: I never work at night
I rarely drink coffee in the evening
variations.changed: rédko, which needs no second negative

mistake.why: The ne is compulsory, not emphasis: Ya nikogdá ne p'yu kófe vécherom.

sentences.usage: Turning down an offer by naming a habit.

words.note: "Now and again" — less often than chásto, more often than rédko. Like nikogdá it ends in -gdá, but unlike nikogdá it changes nothing around it.

sentences.trap: dóma is "at home" and domóy is "to home": one says where you are, the other where you are heading, and neither takes a preposition.
sentences.sound: i-nag-DA ya ra-BO-ta-yu DO-ma. The o of dóma is the stressed one, so the word ends on a clear a rather than a reduced one.

variations.cue: I often work from home
Sometimes I work in the evening

mistake.why: dóma already carries the "at" inside it and refuses a preposition. Inogdá ya rabótayu dóma.

sentences.usage: Explaining an arrangement that is not fixed.

sentences.display: Ya vozvrashcháyus' domóy v shest' chasóv
sentences.script: Я возвращаюсь домой в шесть часов
sentences.cue: I come back home at six o'clock
sentences.literal: I return-self homeward at six of-hours

words.note: The clearest case of a particle that means no self at all — nothing here is returned. It only marks that the verb takes no object, which is what -s' usually does.

sentences.trap: Nothing is given back in this sentence. Handing a thing back to someone is a different verb; vozvrashcháyus' is only about you arriving where you came from.
sentences.sound: vaz-vrash-CHA-yus da-MOY f shest cha-SOF. The stress stays on the stem's -shchá- and the particle is swallowed, as L3's stress law promises.

variations.cue: I come back home late
Usually I come back home early

mistake.display: Ya vozvrashcháyu domóy v shest' chasóv
mistake.script: Я возвращаю домой в шесть часов
mistake.why: Without the particle the verb is transitive and waits for the thing you are giving back. Ya vozvrashcháyus' domóy v shest' chasóv.

sentences.usage: Saying when your working day ends.
sentences.mnemonic: No self in it, and still -s'.

sentences.display: Vécherom ya úzhinayu i chitáyu gazétu
sentences.script: Вечером я ужинаю и читаю газету
sentences.cue: In the evening I have supper and read the paper
sentences.literal: In-the-evening I sup and read paper

words.note: The evening twin of závtrakayu, and a verb for the same reason. Stress on the first syllable, and nothing follows it: what you ate needs its own clause.

sentences.trap: úzhinayu takes no object. The meal is inside the verb, so the food, if you name it, goes in a separate clause joined with i.
sentences.sound: VYE-cha-ram ya U-zhi-na-yu i chi-TA-yu ga-ZYE-tu. Two first-syllable stresses in a row, which is unusual enough to be worth hearing.

variations.cue: In the evening I have supper at home
variations.changed: at home, and the reading dropped

variations.cue: Sometimes I have supper at a café
variations.changed: sometimes, and out at a café

mistake.display: Vécherom ya úzhinayu i chitáyu gazéta
mistake.script: Вечером я ужинаю и читаю газета
mistake.why: The thing read is the object and takes the accusative: chitáyu gazétu.

sentences.usage: Describing an ordinary evening at home.

words.note: Closes a sequence the way snachála opens one. It also works as a standalone exclamation of relief, exactly as English's "finally!" does.

words.cue: I lie down · I go to bed
words.note: Literally "I lay myself down", and Russian keeps spat' after it: lozhús' spat' is the fixed way to say going to bed.

sentences.trap: spat' stays an infinitive after lozhús'. Russian will not let the two verbs both be finite, so "I lie down I sleep" is not available.
sentences.sound: na-ka-NYETS ya la-ZHUS spat. lozhús' takes its stress on the ending, which is where the particle then hangs unstressed.

variations.cue: Finally I go to bed late
Usually I go to bed early
variations.changed: usually and early instead of finally

mistake.why: The particle is what turns "lay" into "lie down": Nakonéts ya lozhús' spat'.

sentences.usage: The last line of an account of your day.

sentences.cue: My sister always wakes up early

words.note: The he/she cell of prosypáyus'. The ending -yet finishes in a consonant, so the particle is the full -sya rather than -s'. The stress does not move.

sentences.trap: -s' and -sya are one particle with two spellings, and the letter in front chooses: a vowel takes -s', a consonant takes -sya. There is nothing else to the rule.
sentences.sound: ma-YA ses-TRA fseg-DA pra-sy-PA-yet-sa. The -tsya is said flat as "tsa", with no y sound in it at all.

variations.cue: My brother always wakes up late
My sister rarely wakes up early

mistake.why: After a consonant the particle is the full -sya: Moyá sestrá vsegdá prosypáyetsya ráno.

comprehensionPool.cue: Usually I drink tea in the morning

comprehensionPool.display: Snachála ya umyváyus', potóm ya odeváyus'
comprehensionPool.script: Сначала я умываюсь, потом я одеваюсь
comprehensionPool.cue: First I wash, then I get dressed
In the evening I have supper at home
My brother always wakes up late
I often read the paper in the evening
I rarely have breakfast at home
